repos.title: Poisson Super Learning For Survival And Competing Risks On A Discretized Time Scale
repos.paper_summary: Poisson Super Learner is an ensemble method for survival and competing-risks prediction with right-censored data. It fits candidate piecewise-constant hazard learners under a shared Poisson likelihood, collects cross-validated log-hazard predictions, and combines them with a Poisson meta learner, producing a geometric ensemble of cause-specific hazards. Survival probabilities and cause-specific absolute risks are derived from these hazards. Each cause gets its own ensemble, and the method does not model the censoring distribution. The candidate library can include parametric, penalised (elastic net), and additive (GAM) learners. The authors report simulation studies and an application to cardiovascular disease risk in patients with type 1 diabetes, using Steno Diabetes Center data from 2005 to 2022. They state that the ensemble performed similarly to the strongest candidate learners across simulated settings, was competitive with existing survival Super Learner approaches and proportional-hazards benchmarks, and remained close to the best individual learner across prediction horizons in the Steno application. The meta-learner coefficients are fixed over time. The authors note that a time-varying meta learner could add instability in intervals with few events. Richer extensions, such as Highly Adaptive Lasso and XGBoost, are listed as future work. The software is the R package poissonsuperlearner.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Poisson Super Learner ensembles candidate hazard learners on a discretized time scale for survival and competing-risks prediction.

digest_headlines.heading: Overview of the Poisson Super Learner
digest_headlines.headline: Candidate hazard learners are trained under Poisson loss, combined by a Poisson meta learner, and mapped to absolute risks.

digest_headlines.heading: General framework
digest_headlines.headline: Piecewise-constant cause-specific hazards give a Poisson log-likelihood, with censoring assumed conditionally independent of event time.

digest_headlines.heading: V-Fold Cross-Validation
digest_headlines.headline: Cross-validated log-hazard predictions are made at subject level so each individual is held out from its own training folds.

digest_headlines.heading: The meta learner
digest_headlines.headline: A time-invariant Poisson meta learner combines base-learner log-hazards into a geometric ensemble hazard.

digest_headlines.heading: The Discrete Poisson Super Learner
digest_headlines.headline: The discrete version selects one learner per cause by minimum cross-validated Poisson loss instead of ensembling.

digest_headlines.heading: Predictions on new data
digest_headlines.headline: Predicted hazards for new covariates combine full-sample base learners, and risks follow from explicit interval formulas.

digest_headlines.heading: Simulation study
digest_headlines.headline: In simulations, the ensemble matched the strongest component learner and library choice mattered under nonlinear hazards.

digest_headlines.heading: Data application on the real data
digest_headlines.headline: In the Steno type 1 diabetes application, the ensemble stayed close to the best individual model across horizons.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion and conclusions
digest_headlines.headline: The ensemble matched its strongest candidates in the tested settings, with time-varying meta learners proposed as a future extension.

digest_headlines.heading: Supplementary material
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix contains closed-form risk derivations, simulation details, supplementary real-data results, and software details.

repos.title: Learning to Falsify: Hierarchical Multiple Instance Learning for High Resolution AI-Generated Image Detection
repos.paper_summary:
Learning to Falsify (LTF) is a hierarchical multiple instance learning detector for AI-generated images that keeps each image at its original resolution. Each image is split into $224\times224$ tiles encoded by a frozen CLIP-ViT. The tile CLS tokens form one tile-level bag, and each tile's patch tokens form a patch-level bag. A gated-attention MIL head aggregates instance logits, and bag predictions are supervised by the image label. Cross-Shuffle recombines instances across images during training, replacing a ratio $\rho<1$ of positions so that fake bags keep at least one fake instance. FATAS is a training-free test-time module that scores tiles with an existing detector and emphasizes the most suspicious ones.

On GenImage, trained on SDv1.4 and tested on eight subsets, LTF averages 98.4% accuracy versus 97.2% for the best listed baseline, PPL. On Midjourney it reaches 97.3%, against 95.3% for SAFE. FATAS raises CNNSpot's Midjourney accuracy by over 20 percentage points and AIDE's Chameleon accuracy by nearly 10.

Limitations: the authors state that LTF is more computationally demanding than single-patch methods, and video detection is left to future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Holistic detectors that resize or crop images can miss local artifacts, especially in high-resolution images.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior detectors resize, crop, or aggregate patches, and local discriminative evidence remains insufficiently modeled.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Learning to Falsify pools tile and patch instances with gated attention, and Cross-Shuffle recombines bags to block image-level shortcuts.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: LTF reaches 81.43 average accuracy on HiRes-50K and 72.94 on Chameleon, and FATAS improves several detectors without retraining.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: LTF generalizes across four benchmarks but costs more computation than single-patch detectors, which the authors leave as future work.

repos.title: CosmosAlpha: Multi-Relational Graph Search with Pareto-Guided Exploration for LLM-Driven Alpha Mining
repos.paper_summary: CosmosAlpha is an LLM-driven framework for formulaic alpha mining that stores evaluated factors as a graph with three edge types: generation lineage, expression-structure similarity (Jaccard overlap of canonical subexpressions), and cross-sectional exposure correlation. Each factor gets three utilities: quality, fertility (its children's hypervolume gain over a frozen Pareto archive), and diversity. Graph Flow propagates these utilities across neighbors with a damping parameter, and non-dominated sorting selects parents for LLM mutation without a fixed scalar weighting. On held-out CSI 300 and CSI 500 test data (2021 to 2025), with factor pools fed into LightGBM, CosmosAlpha-Graph has the best mean rank over seven metrics: 1.43 on CSI 300 and 1.29 on CSI 500. On CSI 300 it beats its MCTS variant on all seven metrics. On CSI 500, Alpha158 leads RankICIR. Limitations: the main runs use one LLM backbone (DeepSeek-V4-Flash), pools are capped at about 150 factors, AlphaJungle had no public implementation so an MCTS proxy is used, and the evaluation covers two A-share universes only.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing LLM factor miners organize search around provenance, so CosmosAlpha instead treats the evaluated factor pool as a multi-relational graph.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work either optimizes factor sets or keeps search history tied to one trajectory, not a shared relational pool.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: CosmosAlpha scores each factor on quality, fertility and diversity, propagates them through a three-relation graph, and selects parents by Pareto fronts.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On CSI 300 and CSI 500, CosmosAlpha-Graph reaches the best mean rank, 1.43 and 1.29, over seven metrics.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The paper reports every ablation trailing the full model on all seven metrics, and the gain holds across LLM backbones and runs.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix covers graph admission, canonical identity, relation construction, archive and fertility formulas, Graph Flow parent selection, metric definitions, and additional result tables.

repos.title: Towards Robust Long-Lived Agents: Benchmarking Experience Lifecycles in Evolving Environments
repos.paper_summary: ReScopeBench is a benchmark for the experience lifecycle of LLM agents in 18 simulated interactive environments, scoring what agents save as reusable memory and skills and how they revise it after silent environment changes. The authors build task streams around shared structural experience (how resources are organized and accessed) and rule experience (reusable constraints), inserting 26 unannounced changes and capping exploration with resource budgets. Each stream runs with and without retained experience. Across 20 models, retained experience raises average task scores (for example, GPT-6 Astra goes from 25.86 to 77.50 with experience). Structural coverage exceeds rule coverage for 17 of 20 models, by a mean of 4.79 points. The best update coverage is 37.63 (Gemini-4-Argon), and the best recovery timeliness is 78.72, so models often recover later than they update immediately. The evaluation uses an LLM judge (GPT-6 Astra), and the scores depend on the private reference rubrics and the simulated environments. Some reported model names and versions are not verifiable from the paper alone.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing benchmarks rarely show which experience agents revise, retain, or lose when environments change silently.

digest_headlines.heading: ReScopeBench
digest_headlines.headline: ReScopeBench builds task streams around shared experience and inserts silent environmental changes that invalidate parts of it.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Experience-enabled scores reach 81.12 at best, but no model exceeds 37.63 in update coverage after change.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work adapts agent experience through reflections, skills, and workflows, while ReScopeBench adds evaluation of how it is maintained under change.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Agents keep much still-valid experience but leave updates incomplete and can fail requests despite correct records.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the 18 environments and 26 scheduled changes, evaluation and judging details, extra analyses, and case studies.

repos.title: OdorSpaces: Visual-Olfactory Embodied Navigation in 3D Environments
repos.paper_summary:
OdorSpaces is a physics-based simulation platform and benchmark for visual-olfactory embodied navigation, in which an agent uses egocentric depth images, gas-density measurements, and pose history to reach an invisible odor source. It augments Habitat-Sim, with scenes from Replica and Matterport3D, by sampling odor fields that Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS) computes in 3D. Two scenarios are defined: propane gas leak and methanol pool fire, where CO2 density stands in as the fire odor. The paper also provides a reference policy: a PPO-trained agent with modality-specific encoders, a fused recurrent memory, and a distance-based reward with a gas-gradient bonus. Training uses a curriculum that raises the initial geodesic distance from 1.5 m to 9.0 m over 30M steps.

On propane, the policy reaches 65.26% SPL on Replica (final distance 1.48 m) and 63.82% on Matterport3D (1.59 m). The strongest baseline, Dual-Recurrent Threshold RL, gets 54.50% and 65.41% SPL. On methanol, the policy reaches 24.72% SPL on Replica and 14.16% on Matterport3D, while rule-based baselines reach 0.00% SPL. Results are over three test seeds. The odor sensor is idealized, odor fields are precomputed, and the benchmark starts after detection rather than covering full plume finding.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: OdorSpaces provides a physics-based benchmark for navigating toward odor sources using vision and gas sensing.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Machine olfaction work mainly addresses semantic odor perception, and source localization methods often use simplified plumes.

digest_headlines.heading: OdorSpaces: A Benchmark for Visual-Olfactory Embodied Navigation
digest_headlines.headline: Agents must reach a hidden odor source within a fixed time budget, using precomputed FDS gas fields in Habitat-Sim scenes.

digest_headlines.heading: Visual-Olfactory Navigation Policy
digest_headlines.headline: A recurrent policy fuses visual, olfactory and pose features and trains with proximal policy optimization.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: The policy has the top mean success-weighted path length in three of four settings; the only exception is Matterport3D propane.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The paper frames OdorSpaces as a first benchmark for this task and lists precomputed fields and idealized sensing as limits.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers FDS settings, scene processing, sensor layout, baseline details, extra ablations, and spawn-distance generalization.

repos.title: EvoWorld: Towards Out-of-Sight World Evolution in Generative Video Models
repos.paper_summary:
EvoWorld is a framework for generating video in which an event changes the world, and the change is shown when the camera returns to a subject that was out of view. The paper also introduces EvoWorld-Data, about 12k generated videos of at least 10 seconds, and EvoWorld-Bench, a 120-case evaluation set. A vision-language model acts as a "brain" that observes each generated segment, tracks the world state, and writes the next prompt. A segment-autoregressive renderer then produces the video, using Identity-Anchored Attention, which biases revisit tokens toward retrieved subject tokens, and a two-stage training scheme: supervised learning with clean anchors, then online rollout training on self-generated context.

On EvoWorld-Bench, EvoWorld reaches 90.8% Core Task Success, which requires successful revisit, event realization, and full causal plausibility together. The best baseline, Evoke-Turbo, reaches 21.7%. EvoWorld scores 100.0% on revisit, 97.5% on event success, and 94.2% on causal plausibility (Evoke: 32.9%). Its visual score of 83.8 is the highest in the table. In the ablation, Core rises from 82.5% without IAA to 84.2% with IAA, and to 90.8% with Stage 2.

Limitations: the benchmark has only 120 cases, and scoring relies on VLM-based judging and verification.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Out-of-sight causal evolution requires video models to reason about event consequences, not only preserve visual history.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Existing long-horizon video models preserve consistency, but do not ensure unobserved worlds keep evolving.

digest_headlines.heading: EvoWorld: Data and Method
digest_headlines.headline: EvoWorld pairs a vision-language model brain with a video renderer, trained on a 12k-video dataset in two stages.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: EvoWorld reaches 90.8% Core Task Success, exceeding the second-best baseline by 69.1 percentage points.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Conclusion: EvoWorld improves out-of-sight causal evolution over recent video world models while keeping quality and consistency.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix covers data construction, benchmark screening, metric definitions, training settings, one-shot baselines, MiniMax-H3 results and limitations.

repos.title: Visual Token Routing: Learning to keep tokens that matter
repos.paper_summary: Visual Token Routing (VTR) is a joint training framework that teaches a vision-language computer-use agent to keep only the visual tokens it needs for its next action. A lightweight spatio-temporal router, a three-layer MLP with 23.3M parameters, reads each image region across the current and previous 10 screenshots and decides whether to keep its token. Kept tokens are scaled by their keep probability so the router receives gradients. Training uses a dual objective: the router minimizes the expected fraction of kept tokens, while an adaptive multiplier keeps the degradation, measured against full-history and anchor-only reference models, at or below 10% of the full history's improvement. Applied to Qwen3.5-2B, VTR matches the dense model on OSWorld, CUA-World, and video game action prediction with 2.5-5.8× fewer visual tokens, and reduces inference cost by up to 3.3× and prefill time by up to 2.9×. On OSWorld it scores 18.1, against 9.4 for H.264 token selection, 5.3 for pixel-diff, and 4.9 for a frozen router. Limitations: results cover one base model and three evaluation settings, and the router is initialized from heuristic labels that use SAM segmentation.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Computer-use agents spend thousands of visual tokens per screenshot, and most of them do not affect the next action.

digest_headlines.heading: Visual Token Routing
digest_headlines.headline: A spatio-temporal router samples keep-or-drop gates per visual token and is trained jointly with the model under an accuracy target.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Qwen3.5-2B is trained on desktop and game data and compared with lower resolution, pixel-difference, codec-based, and frozen-router baselines.

digest_headlines.heading: Results
digest_headlines.headline: VTR matches full-resolution scores on OSWorld, CUA-World, and game clicks with 2.5-5.8 times fewer visual tokens.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Earlier token reduction methods fix the kept-token count in advance or train their selector apart from the action model.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: VTR lets computer-use agents process only the visual tokens they need, cutting inference cost by up to 3.3 times.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists training data, router architecture, joint-training hyperparameters, baseline settings, evaluation protocols, and extra result tables.

repos.title: SpecCompact: Accelerating LLM Agent Context Compaction with Slot-Parallel Semantic Speculative Verification
repos.paper_summary: SpecCompact accelerates context compaction for LLM agents by drafting each summary slot in parallel with a fine-tuned 0.6B drafter (Qwen3-0.6B) and verifying each proposed line with the target model, which accepts the line or writes a local replacement. The six slots follow OpenClaw's schema (Goal, Constraints, Progress, Key Decisions, Next Steps, Critical Context). Verification is binary: a line is accepted when the normalized positive probability is at least 0.7. System optimizations include shared-prefix caching, draft buffering, and line-aware stopping. Against Hermes-style summarization, compaction speedups are 2.04–5.63× across AppWorld, τ3 and LongBench inputs, with Gemma4-31B-IT giving the larger gains. Downstream effects vary by model. With Gemma4, SpecCompact lowers AppWorld Normal TGC from 57.74 to 54.76%. With Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, it raises AppWorld Normal TGC from 28.57 to 33.33%. On RULER, Gemma4 at 8k drops from 71.00 (Target-self) to 66.50. The authors state that SpecCompact does not consistently match target-model summarization in accuracy. Limitations include a 19.6-point lower draft acceptance rate for Qwen3.5 and speedups that shrink on that model. A user study in Hermes reports a median compaction speedup of 8.68×, with latency falling from 63.74 to 7.28 seconds.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Summary slots generated independently can still retain needed information, which motivates parallel compaction.

digest_headlines.heading: Background and Motivation
digest_headlines.headline: Independent slot generation scores 4.73 against 4.44 for monolithic generation across 100 trajectories.

digest_headlines.heading: SpecCompact
digest_headlines.headline: SpecCompact drafts six slots in parallel with a fine-tuned small model, with the target verifying and repairing each line.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: SpecCompact reaches 2.04–5.63x compaction speedups over Hermes, with downstream effects that depend on the target model.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work covers compaction execution and semantic speculation, the two areas SpecCompact combines.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion and Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: SpecCompact shows no consistent accuracy advantage over target summarization, and better drafter alignment may help.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: SpecCompact cuts compaction latency with accuracy trade-offs, and a native Hermes user study confirms the latency benefit.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the drafter prompt, the six slot contracts, and the target verification prompt with its message structure.

repos.title: Doubly-robust causal inference for multi-valued treatment regimes with recurrent neural networks
repos.paper_summary:
This paper extends longitudinal targeted minimum loss-based estimation (LTMLE) to multi-valued treatments by fitting one multinomial treatment model per time point rather than several binary regressions. It uses recurrent neural networks (RNNs) as learners for the outcome, treatment, and censoring models. The target is the expected outcome under static, dynamic, and stochastic treatment rules, identified via the g-formula under sequential unconfoundedness, consistency, and positivity.

In simulations comparing LTMLE and sequential g-computation, each with ensemble machine learning (SL) or RNNs, plus inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), LTMLE with SL or RNNs is approximately unbiased with close to nominal coverage. Sequential g-computation with SL is biased by up to 0.059 under the dynamic rule. Multinomial and binomial treatment models perform similarly with SL, but the multinomial model gives more stable inference with RNN treatment models.

The paper reports under-coverage: LTMLE-RNN covers below nominal at t=36 under the stochastic rule, and LTMLE coverage is lower at later times under the dynamic rule. The authors attribute the RNN under-coverage to optimistic influence-curve variance estimates from networks fit without cross-fitting. Positivity violations remain a concern.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing targeted estimators handle only binary or continuous treatments, so the paper extends LTMLE to multi-valued treatments with recurrent neural networks.

digest_headlines.heading: Motivating example: safety effects of antipsychotic treatment regimes
digest_headlines.headline: Earlier antipsychotic comparisons found lower diabetes risk with haloperidol, olanzapine, and risperidone than with aripiprazole.

digest_headlines.heading: Doubly-robust estimation
digest_headlines.headline: Estimation combines sequential g-computation, inverse probability weighting, and LTMLE, with RNN learners for each nuisance model.

digest_headlines.heading: Simulations
digest_headlines.headline: At month 36, many rule-followers have low cumulative treatment probability under static and dynamic rules, less so with RNNs.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: A multinomial treatment model gives more stable inference than binomial models when treatment models are RNNs.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: LTMLE is approximately unbiased in these simulations, and positivity violations and separate propensity fitting remain open problems.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix gives the data-generating equations, a causal graph figure, and the treatment-effect definitions.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Supporting tables give hyperparameters, metric definitions, performance and positivity results, and computation times for each estimator.

repos.title: Reinforcing End-to-End Autonomous Driving Safety via Negative-Aware Planning in a Unified World-Action Model
repos.paper_summary:
NegWAM is a safety post-training method for unified world-action models (WAMs), which jointly predict future video and driving actions. It starts from a pretrained WAM and adds a second training stage that uses offline-mined failure trajectories. Negatives come from the 16K-trajectory GTRS vocabulary: candidates within 1.0 m ADE of the expert that score zero EPDMS on the NAVSIM v2 metric cache. During training, up to 16 negatives per scene serve as repulsive anchors in a distance-adaptive hinge loss and as clean rider tokens that a contrastive ranking loss scores against the expert. The flow-matching loss stays active, and the riders and scoring head are discarded at inference.

On NAVSIM v2, NegWAM reaches 40.4 EPDMS on navhard, a 4.1% relative gain over the strongest compared scorer-free WAM baseline, and 93.3 EPDMS on navtest. The paper also reports zero-shot closed-loop evaluation on HUGSIM.

Limitations: mining requires an offline EPDMS evaluator and per-scene metric caches, so negative selection depends on privileged evaluation. Only 85.8% of training samples yield at least one valid negative, and the median negative ADE is 0.80 m, with about 9% falling within 0.3 to 0.5 m.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: World-action models learn only from expert trajectories, leaving nearby unsafe alternatives unconstrained, which motivates safety post-training.

digest_headlines.heading: Literature Review
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work shows near-expert failures are useful supervision, but unified world-action models do not explicitly contrast expert trajectories with them.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods
digest_headlines.headline: Near-expert failures mined offline supply repulsive anchor and scene-compatibility losses added to flow-matching post-training.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments and Results
digest_headlines.headline: NegWAM reaches 40.4 EPDMS on navhard and 93.3 on navtest, a 4.1 % relative gain over the strongest scorer-free baseline.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: NegWAM adds no inference overhead, but its generalization to diverse real-world driving remains to be established.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers training configuration, full navtest component scores, additional qualitative cases, failure cases, and limits of the negative supervision.
